summary: Defines how IP and ARP packets are encapsulated for transmission over ARCNET local area networks, using the ARCNET packet header definition standard. It is an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: ARCNET has strict limits on the amount of data each frame can carry. This RFC defines how to send IP and address-resolution messages over ARCNET, including how to split larger packets into fragments.

questions: how is ip sent over arcnet
what is the arp hardware type for arcnet
subtitle: How IP, ARP and RARP packets are carried over ARCNET, including fragmentation and address mapping.

tldr.problem: ARCNET frames carry at most 504 octets of client data. The earlier RFC 1051 method limited unfragmented IP packets to 508 octets.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC places IP, ARP and RARP datagrams in ARCNET client data and uses the ARCNET datalink format to split larger packets into fragments.
tldr.outcome: The method allows up to 120 fragments and replaces RFC 1051. Implementations must configure a smaller packet-size limit for each network.

today: RFC 1201 is an Internet Standard published in February 1991. It obsoletes RFC 1051; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Carrying Internet Packets on ARCNET
sections.content:
RFC 1201 defines how to encapsulate Internet Protocol (IP) and Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) datagrams for ARCNET. It uses the ARCNET Packet Header Definition Standard and replaces the earlier method in RFC 1051.

The RFC also allows Reverse Address Resolution Protocol (RARP) packets to use the same datalink handling as ARP. The datalink places the datagram in the client-data area and divides IP datagrams larger than one frame into fragments.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines how ARCNET carries IP, ARP and RARP packets. It also explains how the datalink splits packets that exceed one frame's capacity.

sections.title: ARCNET Frame Formats
sections.content:
ARCNET provides short frames that are always 256 octets and long frames that are always 512 octets. A short frame can carry 0 to 249 octets of client data; a long frame can carry 253 to 504. An exception frame handles client-data lengths of 250, 251 or 252 octets.

The frame includes hardware and software headers, with padding between them to reach the fixed frame size. The software header carries a protocol identifier, a split flag and a two-octet sequence number. The hardware removes the padding during transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: ARCNET uses fixed-size short and long frames, plus an exception format for three data lengths between them. A software header identifies the protocol and indicates whether the packet is split.

sections.title: Fragmenting and Reassembling Packets
sections.content:
The datalink can split a packet into as many as 120 fragments, each with the same sequence number. An unfragmented packet has a split flag of zero. The first fragment's flag records the total fragment count, and later fragments use flags derived from their position; the fourth fragment, for example, has flag six.

Fragments are sent in order. The receiver may stop reassembly if one arrives out of order or if no further fragment arrives within a few seconds, but it should ignore a repeated fragment. The RFC recommends reserving enough space for the complete packet when the first fragment arrives.

ARCNET hardware reports whether a unicast packet was acknowledged, so implementations are encouraged to retransmit unacknowledged unicast packets or fragments. Broadcast packets are not acknowledged and should not be retransmitted. Retransmission can create duplicates, which IP and ARP can tolerate.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender numbers fragments so the receiver can put them back in order. The receiver ignores duplicates and can abandon reassembly when pieces stop arriving.

sections.title: Mapping IP and ARCNET Addresses
sections.content:
ARCNET addresses are 8 bits, while IP unicast addresses use 32 bits. The RFC recommends using ARP to map a unicast IP address to an ARCNET address rather than configuring matching address suffixes by hand.

All IP broadcast addresses map to ARCNET address 0. ARCNET has no multicast support, so IP multicast addresses also map to address 0. Broadcast packets may be lost, which the RFC says does not have a major effect on IP because IP and ARP do not expect every packet to arrive.

For ARP on ARCNET, the hardware address length is one octet and the ARP hardware type is 7. ARP requests use ARCNET broadcast address 0. The RFC notes that ARCNET addresses can be duplicated on different ARCNET networks and are set by switches rather than fixed in hardware.
sections.plainLanguage: ARP connects an IP address to an ARCNET address. ARCNET uses address 0 for both IP broadcasts and IP multicast, because it has no separate multicast support.

sections.title: Packet Size and Protocol Identifiers
sections.content:
The largest packet this method can carry is 60,480 octets, but the RFC says that size is impractical. All implementations on one ARCNET network must configure and agree on a smaller maximum. They must be able to send and receive IP datagrams up to 576 octets and are strongly encouraged to handle datagrams up to 1500 octets.

A 504-octet IP packet avoids datalink fragmentation, but requires more packets along the path. The RFC suggests that an implementation may use a TCP maximum segment size of 464 octets or announce an IP MTU of 504 octets to other nodes.

Datapoint assigned ARCNET protocol identifiers 212 for IP, 213 for ARP and 214 for RARP. These differ from the identifiers in RFC 1051, so implementations of the two methods can share a network but cannot communicate with one another.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol's theoretical packet maximum is not practical, so devices on one ARCNET network must agree on a configurable limit. The new protocol identifiers also mean this method cannot exchange packets with the older RFC 1051 method.
